title: Lead-Refund Recovery for Home-Service Pros
one_liner: Auto-dispute junk paid leads from Google Local Services, Angi, Thumbtack and Yelp, and take a share of the credits recovered.
customer: HVAC, plumbing, roofing, locksmith, garage-door, pest and electrical firms with 3-30 employees spending $2k-30k a month on paid leads.
problem: A large share of paid leads are spam, wrong-service, out-of-area or duplicates (typically cited at 20-40%; prior knowledge). Disputes are manual and deadline-bound, so owners rarely file. Getting customers is the top small-business challenge, so the spend is untouchable but the waste is fixable.
solution: Connect ad and lead accounts and the phone system's call recordings. Transcribe and classify each lead against each platform's dispute reasons, file disputes with evidence inside the window, track credits, and flag chronically junky sources. A monthly report shows net cost per real lead.
why_now: Cheap call transcription and LLM classification make per-lead review nearly free, and legacy local-marketing vendors are shrinking and raising prices, which raises the value of every recovered credit.
revenue_model: 20-25% of credits recovered (no credit, no fee), or $99/month per account.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody sells lead-refund recovery because each dispute is worth $30-150, but automation turns them into a portfolio. Recovered credits are pure margin for the owner.
first_30_days: Ask 10 contractors from local trade Facebook groups for 90 days of lead exports and call logs. File disputes manually to learn acceptance rates, then automate the top three reason codes.

title: Sewage Nielsen: Wastewater Consumption Index
one_liner: Weekly per-capita consumption of alcohol, nicotine, cannabis and caffeine, measured from metabolites in city wastewater and sold to alt-data funds and regulators as a Nielsen for vices.
customer: Alt-data-buying hedge funds and long-only consumer analysts covering alcohol, tobacco and nicotine pouches, cannabis and energy drinks. Secondary: state cannabis and tax regulators who want to size legal versus illicit share, and cannabis operators or beverage companies buying custom market studies.
problem: Investors debating whether GLP-1 drugs and Gen Z are actually cutting alcohol, or whether nicotine pouches and cannabis are cannibalizing other products, rely on lagging, self-reported or scanner data. Those sources miss the illicit, gray-market, direct-to-consumer and cash segments. Regulators cannot measure the illicit cannabis share either.
solution: Composite-sample assays at 15-25 wastewater treatment plants across major metros, run weekly by a partner analytical lab (LC-MS/MS). Measure alcohol (ethyl sulfate), nicotine (cotinine), cannabis (THC-COOH) and caffeine metabolites. Normalize with population markers and flow to get per-capita consumption estimates. Only report at sewersheds serving 50k+ people, which handles privacy. Deliver as a weekly index via API and CSV with methodology notes. Sell a historical series built from archived samples.
why_now: The GLP-1 alcohol-reduction debate is a live equity question. Nicotine pouches and cannabis regulation are moving fast. Wastewater programs built with pandemic-era public health funding are shrinking or uncertain, which leaves utilities, university labs, sampling gear and freezer archives idle and open to co-funding. Alt-data budgets keep growing and funds want signals with no retail-panel bias.
revenue_model: Alt-data subscription of roughly 60-250k USD per year per fund, with tiered metro coverage. Government and regulator contracts (illicit-market sizing). Custom brand or category studies of 25-100k USD. Later, per-sewershed expansions paid by cities as a public-health co-benefit.
non_obvious_insight: Sewage is the only consumption panel that cannot be gamed, self-reported or missed by scanner data, because it captures what people actually consume regardless of channel. The science has been used by European drug-monitoring networks for 15 years, but nobody has packaged it as a consumer-sector economic indicator. Pandemic-era freezer archives of stored samples let you sell a multi-year backtestable history on day one, which is the thing quant buyers require before they will pay.
first_30_days: Partner with a university lab that already has validated LC-MS/MS methods for these metabolites and old COVID-monitoring relationships with treatment plants. Sign MOUs with 3-5 plants. Run assays on archived samples to build a 2021-2025 backtest series for those sewersheds. Pitch 15 alt-data funds and data-aggregator marketplaces with the backtest chart of one hook (for example alcohol per-capita against local retail sales). Launch a pilot at 5 sewersheds with 2-3 design-partner funds paying pilot fees. Note that the plan depends on plant access agreements and lab throughput.

title: Rate-Leak Evidence Packs for Independent Hotels
one_liner: Mystery-shopping plus payout reconciliation that proves when OTA and reseller channels sold below the rate a hotel loaded, packaged as evidence for claims and regulator complaints.
customer: Independent hotels of 20-200 rooms in the EU, UK and US that rely on OTA merchant-model bookings, and hotel associations. The second buyer is a law firm or litigation funder that needs evidence to build a case.
problem: 51% of European hotels say OTAs sell below their loaded rate (up from 40% two years ago), Booking.com handles 66.1% of OTA bookings at surveyed hotels, and 26% of hotels do not know whether rates are passed on. A hotel loads $200, the guest sees $180, and the hotel is paid after checkout. Markups by Agoda, Citi, AA and Southwest loyalty portals are invisible to rate-shopping tools. The only party able to audit the markup is the one being audited.
solution: A panel of real-guest shoppers and reseller-portal quotes covers the hotel's next 90 dates. The results are reconciled against the hotel's folios and payout statements into a 'leak ledger' (date, channel, price shown vs loaded, payout). Timestamped, tamper-evident captures go into a monthly report and an evidence pack the hotel can hand to counsel, an association, a regulator (the EU DMA parity ban) or a claims funder.
why_now: The DMA (Booking designated a gatekeeper in 2024) bans parity clauses, so hotels have new legal options but no proof. The merchant model keeps growing. Fuel and energy shocks (Hormuz, March 2026) and a K-shaped market squeeze lower-tier independents, so recoveries matter.
revenue_model: About EUR 149 per property per month, plus a 20% contingent share of any recovery through a partner law firm or funder. Anonymized leak indices are sold to associations.
non_obvious_insight: The evidence does not exist until someone captures it in real time, and it is perishable because prices change hourly. The firm holding a year of timestamped leaks holds the case file, and OTA self-reporting can never be independent.
first_30_days: Partner with one regional hotel association (Spain, Italy or Croatia). Run a manual 30-date shop of Booking, Expedia, Agoda and two loyalty portals for 20 hotels, and deliver a one-page 'leak map'. Sell a one-off audit at EUR 300, convert 3-5 hotels to the subscription, and take the pack to one litigation funder as proof of concept.

title: Tariff Exposure Radar by House Plan
one_liner: A per-plan bill-of-materials scan that flags the small imported, tariff-exposed slice of inputs, prices the swing and proposes lower-exposure substitutes.
customer: Purchasing managers and owners at regional and mid-size builders (100-2,000 homes a year), remodelers, and building-material dealers. Distribution via home builders associations.
problem: NAHB estimates tariffs add $10,900 per home and Brookings sees about $30B added to residential construction and renovation cost by 2027. Only about 7% of inputs are imported, but they are mostly items with no quick domestic substitute, and reported lumber and steel tariff rates conflict across sources. Builders reprice by gut, sign fixed-price contracts blind, and have no per-plan exposure number.
solution: Ingest plan takeoffs and supplier price lists, map each SKU to country of origin and tariff line, and compute exposure per plan and per option package. Deliver escalation-clause language for buyer and sub contracts, alerts when rates change, substitute suggestions from domestic or alternate-origin catalogs, and a group-buy on substitutes.
why_now: Tariff rates are moving and sources disagree. Builder margins are gone (63% use incentives), so a $10K per-home swing decides whether a plan pencils. Structured plan data is now available from design-automation tools.
revenue_model: $500-2,000 per month per builder. $1,500 one-off plan audits. 2-4% rebate on substituted spend from group buys.
non_obvious_insight: Because most of a house is domestic, the tariff burden is a short list of SKUs, so the right tool is a narrow, boring lookup rather than a global trade-compliance platform. The money is in plan-level re-spec and escalation clauses, not in customs filings.
first_30_days: Offer 10 builders a free top-40 exposed-SKU audit from their last three takeoffs and supplier quotes. Send a one-page report and convert 3 to paid. Get a slot in a regional builders association newsletter.

title: Camera Sentinels for Screwworm on Ranches
one_liner: Solar cameras at water troughs and chutes that flag wounded animals early, so ranchers can act before quarantine.
customer: Texas and Southern cattle ranchers, feedyards and stockyards, plus livestock insurers.
problem: New World screwworm is confirmed in Texas cattle and wound checks on huge pastures are impossible with scarce labor, while one missed case can trigger quarantine and lost sales.
solution: Cellular solar cameras with computer vision fine-tuned on wound and head-shaking images, alerts with geotags, and exportable inspection logs to support movement documentation.
why_now: Confirmed screwworm in Texas, a Mexican feeder-cattle halt removing about 1.2M head a year, and record cattle values make early detection worth real money.
revenue_model: $40-90 per camera per month plus installation, with possible insurer and state-program subsidies.
non_obvious_insight: You are selling regulatory insurance rather than analytics: the asymmetry of one undetected case versus a daily-check labor bill makes even a noisy sentinel valuable.
first_30_days: Install about 20 off-the-shelf trail cameras on five Texas ranches, collect wound imagery with local vets, and run a 30-day alert pilot billed per camera.

title: Cool-Cap Ledger: Indoor Temperature Evidence for Landlords
one_liner: Low-cost sensors and tamper-evident logs that give landlords, tenants and inspectors one accepted reading of indoor temperature.
customer: Owners and property managers of 10+ unit buildings in Maryland (80F cap since June 1 2026), LA County (82F from Jan 1 2027) and NYC (78F cap, owner duty from 2030). Tenant groups and code enforcement are secondary buyers.
problem: Cooling caps are enforced by complaint, so the fight will be over readings: a tenant's phone app against a landlord with no record. Landlords face fines and habitability suits with no defensible data, and tenants cannot prove violations.
solution: $30 sensors in a sampled set of units, third-party-verifiable logs, a tenant-visible dashboard, automated compliance reports and a dispute-response pack. An upsell is a unit-level cooling-gap map for capex planning, showing which units to retrofit first under LA County's phase-in.
why_now: Maryland's cap is already live, LA County starts in about 3 months, and NYC Local Law 2026/023 is passed. The summer 2026 heat set off a wave of complaints.
revenue_model: $4-8 per unit per month for landlords, plus municipal enforcement licenses.
non_obvious_insight: In a complaint-driven regime, evidence is the product. Neutral data protects landlords from false claims and tenants from real violations, so both sides will accept it.
first_30_days: Sign 5-10 LA County and Maryland property managers for winter pilots ahead of the Jan 2027 start. Build the logging and report pack, and pilot in 100 units.

title: Whisper Director for Immersive Theatre and LARP
one_liner: Beacon badges plus an AI conductor that whispers real-time cues to human actors so a 100-guest immersive show feels individually authored.
customer: Immersive theatre companies, escape-room chains, LARP organizers, corporate murder-mystery producers, and Meow Wolf-style venues.
problem: Immersive magic depends on actors responding to each guest, but no actor can track 100 people. Guests get generic loops, and shows stay small and unprofitable. Meow Wolf's Los Angeles and New York venues and Sphere's $420.5M gross show the demand.
solution: Version 1 is a stage-manager console. Guests wear BLE or UWB badges, software tracks paths and story flags, and an LLM plus rules engine produces cue whispers for performers via bone-conduction earpieces. There are no AI actors, only human performers with better information. Start with 40-person murder-mystery dinners and LARPs.
why_now: Low-latency LLMs and voice models, cheap beacons, and a live-experience boom make this feasible now, and the market is pushing toward permanent immersive venues.
revenue_model: $300-1,500 per production week, $5 per guest hardware rental, and licences for permanent installs.
non_obvious_insight: AI in entertainment is aimed at replacing performers, but the constrained resource in immersive theatre is coordination bandwidth, not talent. Human performers plus a conductor scales what audiences pay for.
first_30_days: Partner with 3 immersive producers or LARP groups. Rent BLE tags and run a 15-person cast pilot at a Halloween or winter event. Sell paid pilots at $2-4k per event.

title: Indonesia Halal Rescue for Food Exporters
one_liner: A fast-track service that gets mid-size food, supplement and cosmetics exporters registered and documented under Indonesia's mandatory halal regime, then keeps them compliant.
customer: Mid-size US, EU and Australian exporters and their Indonesian importers, plus halal certifiers who white-label the work.
problem: Halal certification becomes mandatory for imported food, beverages, cosmetics and supplements on 17 Oct 2026, with enforcement from 18 Oct. The authority says no extensions, certification takes 3-6 months, and USDA FAS (Sept 2026) flags roughly $2.5B of US ag exports affected. Many mid-size firms treat halal as a marketing label and have not started.
solution: A gap analysis, supplier halal-declaration collection, matching to recognized foreign halal bodies, registration filing, and label and claim review. A software ledger tracks every ingredient and supplier certificate across SKUs and alerts on expiry, which also serves kosher and EU documentation needs.
why_now: The cliff is three weeks away and the lead time exceeds that, so late movers face shipment holds. After the deadline the work shifts to cure (relabeling, re-filing, clearing stuck shipments), which is recurring.
revenue_model: $4-15k per SKU-family project plus $500-2k/month monitoring, and certifier white-label fees.
non_obvious_insight: Halal has become a customs gate rather than a marketing certificate, so budgets come from logistics and compliance, not brand. The ingredient-and-supplier documentation ledger is reusable across regimes.
first_30_days: Email and LinkedIn outreach to 300 exporters from USDA export directories and state trade offices, offering a $750 48-hour readiness check. Partner with 1-2 recognized halal bodies and prioritize firms with shipments already in transit.

title: Orphaned Job and Membership Rescue Desk
one_liner: When a PE roll-up of contractors collapses, package its unfinished jobs, prepaid maintenance memberships and warranties and hand them to healthy local contractors, while lenders and trustees get paid for the recovery.
customer: Two payers. (1) Private-credit lenders, Chapter 11 trustees and creditor committees of collapsed home-service platforms, on a success fee. (2) Local independent contractors and newly formed tech-owned shops, who pay a per-customer transfer fee to inherit service obligations and customer relationships.
problem: Roll-ups of HVAC, remodeling and roofing firms are failing, and the stranded parties have no one to coordinate. Homeowners are left with half-finished jobs and prepaid plans. Laid-off technicians hold the customer relationships but not the customer data. Lenders are owed $100M+ from shells with almost no assets and have no operating capability to finish jobs and collect receivables.
solution: A rapid-response playbook plus lightweight software: (1) an intake site for stranded customers ('my contractor shut down'); (2) an import of the estate's job, warranty and membership data from its field-service or CRM exports, scored by job stage, deposit status, and geography; (3) matching to vetted local contractors, with milestone escrow so the deposit follows the work; (4) a lender/trustee dashboard showing completed WIP and recovered receivables. A starter kit (entity formation, insurance, licensing checklist, FSM software setup) lets laid-off technicians become buyers of the books they used to serve.
why_now: 2025 was a record year for PE-linked distress. The PE Stakeholder Project counts PE firms in 19 of the 35 largest US bankruptcies (54%) and 21 of 41 large ones (51%) in 2025, though it is an advocacy source. Bain's 2026 reports say borrowing costs are 8-9% versus 6-7% a decade ago, and deals now need 10-12% annual EBITDA growth to hit target returns. That squeezes leveraged service roll-ups. Private credit, not banks, now holds much of the paper, and these lenders lack turnaround operations for field-service businesses.
revenue_model: 5-10% success fee on WIP completed and receivables recovered for the estate. $150-400 per customer transferred, paid by the acquiring contractor. Optional 1-1.5% escrow fee on consumer deposits. Subscription for lenders who want a watchlist and pre-built playbook.
non_obvious_insight: In a roll-up collapse the valuable asset is the unfulfilled service obligations (prepaid memberships, warranties, half-built jobs), not the brand or customer list. Local independents will pay to inherit them, and lenders recover more from orderly completion than from a liquidation. Renovo, formed in 2021 by Audax by combining three home-remodeling businesses (later seven), filed in November 2025 with about $50,000 in assets against more than $100M in liabilities, after roughly $150M from BlackRock, Apollo and Oaktree. About 1,500 workers were terminated, some without final paychecks, and homeowners were left with incomplete projects. Cutting installer pay from 10-12% to 8% drove out skilled workers (https://pestakeholder.org/private-equity-bankruptcy-tracker/). In September 2026 PE-backed United Air Temp (Littlejohn's United Comfort Group, eight partner companies) filed WARN notices for 135+ layoffs across VA and MD, closing its Lorton HQ effective Nov 10, 2026 (https://www.achrnews.com/articles/166687-private-equity-backed-united-air-temp-announces-mass-layoffs). WARN notices are a free, public lead source for the next rescue.
first_30_days: Build a watchlist from public WARN notices and bankruptcy dockets for home-service platforms. Stand up a 'my contractor shut down' landing page and intake form for one distressed metro. Sign 5 local independent contractors who agree to take transferred customers at a flat fee. Cold-approach restructuring counsel and Chapter 11 trustees at 5-10 private-credit special-situations desks with a free 2-week pilot on a small estate. Estate authority over customer data will be the gating legal step, so line up a bankruptcy attorney early.

title: Second-opinion technical review for city data center deals
one_liner: A fixed-fee package for small cities facing a data center: adversarial review of the developer's noise, water and power submissions, plus a term sheet built from the few community benefit agreements that exist.
customer: Planning directors, city managers and county administrators in jurisdictions under a data center moratorium or first inquiry, mostly populations of 5k-150k that cannot afford a big-firm consultant. They pay $8k-25k per package, and the cost can often be recovered from the applicant through an escrow for third-party review.
problem: Small governments are negotiating blind against developers' consultants. Broken Arrow, OK issued an RFQ for consultants to 'advise on environmental, water, noise, utilities and fiscal modeling' and needs recommendations by year-end 2026 or a moratorium extension. Fort Worth voted unanimously for a moratorium, Chicago introduced one in September 2026, and Lexington, KY paused approvals until at least Oct 31, 2026. NPR reports that deals such as the one in Boyce, Louisiana were negotiated under NDAs. The Federation of American Scientists found only eight executed community benefit agreements, only one fully executed and publicly posted (Lancaster, PA), and says 'best practices are not readily available'.
solution: A productized package. (1) An ordinance with fill-in standards: setbacks, dBA limits at the property line, closed-loop or reclaimed-water requirements, decommissioning bond, and utility-capacity verification. (2) A fiscal calculator comparing abatement to service and infrastructure costs, plus water/wastewater and power-interconnection checks. (3) A term-sheet library annotated from the known executed CBAs. (4) A retained on-call review of the developer's noise study, water plan and load forecast by contract engineers, with a plain-language memo the council can read in open session. Moratorium end dates are natural deadlines that pull purchases forward.
why_now: Data center siting became the top local land-use fight of 2026: Wixom MI, Denver, Fort Worth, San Antonio, Lexington, Broken Arrow and Chicago all acted this year, and more cities keep opening moratorium clocks. Developer NDAs are now a political issue, which pushes officials to buy independent review.
revenue_model: $8k-25k fixed fee per package; $2.5k/month retainer during active negotiation; per-review fee for developer-funded escrow; a subscription comparables database (abatement terms, water allocations, decommissioning bonds) for state municipal leagues.
non_obvious_insight: Ordinance templates are free and cities can copy them; the scarce thing is an adversarial reader of the developer's technical submissions, because the city's only counterpart is the developer's own consultants under NDA. Applicant-funded escrow lets the city avoid a budget fight, so procurement is quick. Evidence: Broken Arrow's RFQ scope and year-end deadline (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9481196/oklahoma/tulsa-county/broken-arrow/city-council-meetings/city-forms-datacenter-study-committee-says-ordinance-moratorium-remains-in-place); the gap in best practices and only eight executed CBAs (https://fas.org/publication/data-center-community-benefit-agreements/); NDA-shrouded deals (https://www.npr.org/2026/08/27/nx-s1-5879528/data-center-nda-disclosure-louisiana); Fort Worth's unanimous moratorium (https://fortworthreport.org/2026/08/12/data-center-moratorium-takes-first-steps-after-fort-worth-city-councils-unanimous-vote/).
first_30_days: Publish a free comparison of the eight known CBAs and a one-page 'questions to ask a data center developer' for planning directors. Email 30 planning directors in cities with moratoria expiring in the next 6 months. Line up 2 retired utility or acoustic engineers as contract reviewers. Sell 2 fixed-fee review memos at $6k each, ideally funded by the applicant's escrow.

title: Philanthropic First-Loss Pool for Vet Care Loans
one_liner: Use foundation money as a loan guarantee instead of a grant, so each philanthropic dollar backs many dollars of low-APR vet credit that recycles as owners repay.
customer: Credit unions and CDFIs (lenders), private foundations (guarantee capital via program-related investments), and clinics (merchant side). End borrowers are middle-income owners who decline care.
problem: The briefing says 13% of euthanasias are attributed to inability to pay, and half of owners would be stressed by a bill of $1,000 or less. Options today are deferred-interest cards with 30%-plus APRs after the promo period, or subprime fintech loans. New philanthropy (Duffield $250M over 5 years; first grants are 250 x $10K) can't fund per-case care one grant at a time.
solution: A 'Care Guarantee Pool': a foundation funds a first-loss reserve (say 10-15% of a loan portfolio). A partner credit union or CDFI originates fixed-rate installment loans of $500-$5,000 at the clinic front desk, and the clinic is paid in about 48 hours. The vet's treatment plan is attached as collateral evidence to limit fraud, with an option to assign insurance proceeds. We run the program: clinic onboarding, application flow, servicing data and outcome reporting ('pets treated instead of euthanized').
why_now: The Duffield Foundation committed $250M on 2026-09-17, on top of PetSmart Charities' $100M pledge. Funders are looking for leverage and measurable outcomes. Embedded-lending rails (bank-as-a-service, instant payouts) make a lender-agnostic origination flow cheap to build.
revenue_model: 1-2% annual program-management fee on guaranteed balances (paid by the foundation), 2-3% origination fee from clinics, and a servicing share from the lender. Later, licensing of performance data.
non_obvious_insight: Philanthropy frames access as a subsidy problem. For the many owners who would repay an $1,800 bill over 12 months at 8% but face 30% APR or a deferred-interest trap, it is a cost-of-capital problem. A guarantee makes a one-shot grant a revolving fund, and it gives funders the proof they crave.
first_30_days: Get an LOI from one credit union or CDFI. Recruit 3 affordable-care clinics in one metro. Pitch a local community foundation and PetSmart Charities for a $250K pilot reserve (roughly $2M of loans). Use the lender's existing loan-origination software plus a simple clinic link. Model expected loss from 12-month payment-plan data at the clinics.

title: Service-Linked Loans for Vet Students Facing Caps
one_liner: Grad PLUS ended for new borrowers on July 1, 2026, and vet school now hits a $50K-per-year, $200K aggregate federal cap; clinics and rural practices can fill the gap with work-linked financing that doubles as retention.
customer: First- and second-year DVM students at high-cost programs (borrowers), and clinic groups, rural food-animal practices and state programs (employers who fund the retention hook).
problem: Veterinary medicine is one of 11 professional programs under the new caps, and out-of-state or private DVM costs can exceed $200K over four years, so students will lean on pricier private loans or cosigners. Meanwhile employers pay sign-on bonuses with no retention hook, and rural and food-animal practices cannot recruit; only 1.3% of vets are in food-animal practice, and South Texas is under strain from screwworm.
solution: A gap-financing product where employers pre-commit to fund a student's tuition gap in exchange for a 3-5 year service commitment with vesting forgiveness (like health-service scholarships). We underwrite, originate through a bank or CDFI partner, and administer vesting, recourse and state-incentive stacking, including Texas' funded rural veterinary incentive program.
why_now: The first cohort under the caps is enrolling this fall. Roll-ups are hungry for associates, Texas has funded rural vet incentives, and screwworm has made food-animal vet scarcity visible to policymakers.
revenue_model: 1-2% origination plus an annual administration fee paid by employers (8-12% of loan balance vested), and a spread on the loan book.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders see loan caps as a schools' problem. The second-order effect is that caps create a class of employers willing to pay to lock scarce DVMs four years early, turning tuition into the cheapest recruiting channel the industry has had.
first_30_days: Interview financial-aid officers at 4 high-cost schools. Sign term sheets with 3 employers (a rural practice group, a regional corporate group, a state program). Line up one bank or CDFI partner and get legal review on income-share and recourse rules in 3 states. Pilot with 10 students.

title: Pre-Registered Neighbor Impact Studies for Data Centers
one_liner: A neutral 'testing lab' for whether a data center, battery plant or transmission line lowers nearby home values, with the method locked and published before anyone sees the results.
customer: Four payers. (1) Data center, BESS, solar and transmission developers facing moratoria or rezoning hearings pay $15-60k per study. (2) County and city planning departments and utility commissions pay $10-40k for a neutral study. (3) Resident coalitions and HOAs pay $3-8k for a 'lite' study, usually crowdfunded. (4) Landowner condemnation and easement attorneys.
problem: Every land-use fight ends in dueling consultant reports. Developer studies use hand-picked matched pairs that always show 'no impact'. Residents bring anecdotes. Planning staff can't judge either side, so boards vote on vibes and moratoria spread. Nobody trusts any report, so the reports are worthless.
solution: A repeatable, pre-registered protocol. Step 1: publish (timestamped and hashed) the analysis plan, including radius bands, event dates and exclusion rules. Step 2: pull every arm's-length sale within 0.25 to 2 miles, before and after the announcement date and the operation date. Step 3: run a repeat-sales difference-in-differences or synthetic-control analysis against similar areas that had no project. Step 4: have a licensed appraiser review every sale for arm's-length status, condition and segment (estates, REO and investor flips get pulled), and do a ground visit for what is actually audible and visible from the homes. Step 5: deliver a USPAP-compliant consulting report plus an interactive map. Results are published whichever way they come out. Add a 5-year 'impact monitor' subscription for counties and developers that tracks post-operation sales.
why_now: AI-driven data center siting in 2025-26 has produced local moratoria, rezoning denials and noise complaints in many states (VA, GA, TX, AZ, IN, OH). Property values are one of the top arguments alongside power and water. Federal and state pushes to speed up transmission and energy siting mean more condemnation and easement fights. Public sales data plus cheap compute make a rigorous study a $10k job instead of a $100k one.
revenue_model: Fixed-fee studies, paid upfront into escrow so the client cannot steer the result. Annual retainers for repeat developers (for example 8-10 sites a year). $10-15k/yr monitoring subscriptions for counties. Later, an 'Impact Study Standard' certification that planning codes can reference.
non_obvious_insight: Appraisers know matched-pair studies are the hired gun's favorite toy: pick 6 pairs that support the client and you're done, and both sides know it. Credibility is the scarce input, not analysis. Pre-registration is standard in clinical trials and unheard of in appraisal. Developers will pay for a study that might go against them, because a study nobody believes is worth nothing at a hearing. The other secret is timing. Buyer perception moves at announcement, before the first shovel, so studies run only on 'after operation' miss the effect. A difference-in-differences on the announcement date catches it.
first_30_days: Pick one hot metro (for example Northern Virginia or metro Atlanta). Run a free 'shadow study' on existing data centers there using public sales records, with the method pre-registered on a public page. Email planning directors, 10 resident groups and 5 developer permitting leads. Recruit two appraisers as signing reviewers. Aim to sign one $12-20k study, or a county pilot, by day 30-45.

title: Real-Pixel Blink Fixer for Family Formals
one_liner: A Lightroom/Photoshop plugin that turns a 5-frame burst of the 30-person family formal into one frame where every set of eyes is open, using only real pixels from the burst and no generated faces.
customer: Solo and small-studio wedding photographers (roughly 100k in the US), paying $29-49/mo or about $2 per composite. Later extension: school, team, church and corporate group-portrait photographers.
problem: Family formals are the 20-40 minute block of the day that grandparents care about most. They are also mathematically hostile. If each person has their eyes closed about 8% of the time, a 30-person frame has under a 10% chance of everyone being open, before counting people who look away or squint. So the delivered frame is nearly always a compromise or a composite. Photographers either hand-swap heads in Photoshop (20-40 minutes per group, or $15-40 per image if outsourced), ship the frame with the blinker, or use generative fill. Generative fill invents a face, which is a betrayal when the face is a grandfather who won't be there in two years.
solution: Drop in the formals folder. The tool groups frames into bursts, aligns them (people shift between frames), scores each person's face for eyes open, smile, gaze and sharpness, picks the best patch per person, and blends with seam-aware masks. The output is a layered PSD so the photographer can override any face in one click. The pitch is a strict 'zero generative pixels' guarantee. A second mode is a shoot-time phone companion that says 'frame 3 has 2 blinkers, shoot one more' so bursts are captured with enough variety. The wedge is batch mode for formals only, not a full editor.
why_now: Google's Best Take (Pixel 8, 2023) taught consumers to expect a merged best-expression group photo. Photographers already pay monthly for AI culling and editing, so AI tooling is normal spend in this trade. Adobe's own face-swap route leans on generative fill, which many pros distrust for client faces. On-device face-landmark and eye-state models are now cheap and accurate enough to run locally on a laptop. Searches in Sept 2026 found only manual Photoshop tutorials for this, not a dedicated automated burst-composite product.
revenue_model: Subscription of $29/mo for solo shooters or $2 per composite credit with monthly bundles. Studio plans at $79/mo. Optional white-label API for gallery platforms (Pic-Time, ShootProof-type) later.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody outside the trade realizes that a truly 'perfect' 30-person frame almost never exists in a single exposure, so every delivered formal is quietly a fix or a compromise. The fix that matters is provenance: the people who print the formals at 16x20 are the elderly relatives, and they will notice an AI-invented face on Grandpa. 'Real pixels only' is the actual feature, not the face-swapping.
first_30_days: Build against Lightroom Classic/Photoshop with open-source face-landmark models. Ask 20 photographers in Facebook groups and r/WeddingPhotography to send 3 old formals bursts from past weddings (every working shooter has hundreds sitting in archives). Return composites in 24 hours with before/after slider pages. First 10 composites free, then $2 each via Stripe. Post the before/afters and blink-probability math in photographer communities. Goal is 30 paying studios and one gallery-platform partnership conversation by day 90.

title: Private Set Intersection Mule Graph for Credit Unions
one_liner: Let hundreds of small banks and credit unions ask 'has anyone flagged this payee account?' without revealing customers or lists, using cryptographic private set intersection.
customer: Credit unions and community banks, sold through CUSOs, leagues and core processors, plus fintech sponsor banks.
problem: One account takeover can send 50+ ACH transfers to accounts at multiple banks, and each bank sees only its slice. Large-institution consortia dominate, and smaller institutions avoid sharing because of privacy, liability and competitive-leakage worries, even though information-sharing rules (314(b)) allow it.
solution: A pre-payment check API and core-integration widget. A payee's hashed account and routing data is checked via private set intersection against the pool of accounts members have flagged, returning hit count, recency and fraud category without exposing either side's lists. It adds burst alerts that notify other members when a takeover is in progress and automates the compliance paperwork.
why_now: Open-source PSI libraries and confidential-compute services have matured. The FBI freeze data exposed the cross-bank blind spot, Socure's $5.2B valuation shows the market's value, and FedNow adoption is reaching smaller institutions.
revenue_model: $500-5K per month per institution by asset size, and per-check fees for fintechs.
non_obvious_insight: Banks decline to share data because of liability and competitive leakage, not indifference. Cryptography removes the objection without asking anyone to trust a vendor with their data, and the network effect is regional, so a single state league can seed it.
first_30_days: Talk to a state credit-union league and recruit 5 pilot credit unions. Seed with confirmed-fraud lists they already hold, build the API on open-source PSI, and sign letters of intent for paid rollout.

title: Bench-Truth Diligence for Biotech Investors
one_liner: Sell seed VCs, pharma BD teams and AI-bio founders confidential 'does this paper's key result actually work?' intelligence, from anonymous postdoc consensus polls up to paid replication of the one key experiment.
customer: Seed and Series A biotech VCs, corporate venture arms, pharma BD and scouting teams evaluating academic spinouts or in-licensing, and AI-bio startups building on published wet-lab claims. Pay $4-6k for a poll-only memo and $15-40k for a key-experiment replication.
problem: Investors and BD teams can't tell which high-profile papers replicate. The truth exists as hallway consensus: 'that result only works in the first author's hands', 'nobody outside that lab can get the organoid protocol to run', 'cells were cultured as previously described' with four layers of citations. Formal diligence hires KOL consultants who are conflicted and often the PI's friends, or a CRO that needs 4 months and a full protocol. Bad academic-asset bets burn $5-20M before anyone notices.
solution: Wedge product 'Bench Pulse': in 5 business days, poll 8-15 vetted, paid, anonymous postdocs and senior techs working in the exact subfield about the named claim, reagents and protocol. Deliver a structured memo with consensus, red flags, the Figure-3 problem, which reagents or lots are fragile, and a 'what to test first' plan. Upsell: 'Key-Figure Replication'. A pool of laid-off or between-position scientists runs the single decisive experiment in 3-4 weeks in rented bench space (not on university property), with pre-registered success criteria and blinded readout.
why_now: Biotech funding since 2023 rewards capital efficiency, so seed funds want cheaper, faster kill decisions. Pharma is shopping for early assets in academia and abroad. AI-bio companies are building on published wet-lab claims with little bench sense. NIH disruption and biotech layoffs have released a large pool of very good bench scientists who want paid, flexible work. Expert-network compliance norms are now well understood, so a compliant structure is feasible.
revenue_model: Fixed-fee per poll memo and per replication study. Annual retainer for funds that want a pipeline-wide 'bench pulse' (about $30-60k). Optional success-fee or advisory equity for AI-bio startups.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not lab capacity, it is candid consensus. Replication is expensive, but the postdoc informal network already knows which labs' results hold up. The winning move is to monetize that gossip compliantly and only spend on replication after the poll narrows the question. GLG-style expert calls fail because they interview one conflicted senior person instead of 10 juniors who actually do the pipetting.
first_30_days: Choose one subfield you personally have 20 contacts in (for example CAR-T, organoids, targeted protein degradation or spatial biology). Build the compliant NDA plus anonymity protocol with a lawyer for about $3k. Offer 3 seed funds a free poll on one asset they are already looking at. Convert the fund that reacts to a paid $5k poll, then upsell one replication. Pay panelists $150-300 per poll from the first revenue.

title: Result-Loop Desk for Scan and Lab Startups
one_liner: An outsourced nurse-and-radiologist desk that closes the loop on abnormal results from full-body scans, MCED tests and mega-panels.
customer: Mid-tier consumer diagnostics operators without downstream care: full-body MRI resellers, regional imaging centers, longevity clinics, mega-panel labs and employer executive-health programs.
problem: A review of 12 studies found 95% of asymptomatic people had at least one abnormal whole-body MRI finding and 91% of those were not clinically relevant (15-30% false-positive rate). Primary-care waits average ~31 days, so patients arrive at their PCP with printouts. Adoption is accelerating (Neko $700M for a NYC launch, Function 1M+ members), and Lp(a) testing hit a wall when Lp(a)HORIZON failed on Sep 4, 2026, leaving many flagged people without a next step.
solution: Triage each flagged result (ignore, repeat in X months, refer), track follow-up imaging against nodule and lesion guidelines, produce a structured PCP handoff (FHIR), document loop closure and route to a price-transparent cash referral network. Sold as a risk-management service. Consumers can buy a $99 second-opinion review.
why_now: Elective screening boomed in 2025-26 (Function-Ezra, Neko US launch, MCED tests despite NHS-Galleri missing its primary endpoint in May 2026). Medscape and radiology press now describe a 'medical cascade', so reputation and liability risk are becoming visible to operators.
revenue_model: $40-150 per flagged member (B2B), plus annual tracking fee per incidental finding, plus consumer second-opinion upsell.
non_obvious_insight: Screening companies are paid at the scan, but the costs of false positives and lost follow-ups land months later on nobody. Because they are not care providers, they cannot build the follow-up function in-house, so it converts to a compliance product.
first_30_days: Sell a pilot to three regional imaging centers or longevity clinics that resell whole-body MRI. Staff one part-time radiologist and one RN navigator, run follow-up tracking with SMS and a spreadsheet, and charge $75 per flagged patient. Publish a 'follow-up leakage' audit as the sales asset.

title: Independent Inspections for AI-Built Software
one_liner: A third-party inspection-and-certificate service, staffed by displaced senior engineers, that tells buyers, lenders and insurers what is really inside AI-generated apps before money changes hands.
customer: Buyers of micro-SaaS and small apps on acquisition marketplaces (deals $20k-$2M), SMBs whose apps were built by vibe-coding freelancers, seed investors doing diligence and lenders financing software purchases.
problem: Insiders say AI made software cheap, but the cost moved to trust. Marketplaces are filling with prompt-built products of unknown security, licensing and maintainability, and misconfigured database rules in AI-generated apps have been reported. Traditional code audits cost $10-50k and take weeks. Meanwhile senior devs sit unemployed for many months.
solution: A fixed-price 48-hour 'app inspection': automated scans (secrets, dependency licences, database access rules, auth and PII flows) plus a 2-4 hour senior human review. The output is a standardised graded report like a home-inspection report, with repair-cost estimates and a maintainability score. Inspectors are paid $500-900 each, and an optional badge can be accepted by escrow agents.
why_now: The vibe-coding boom in 2025-26 flooded acquisition marketplaces with AI-built listings, agentic scanners make the first pass nearly free, and unemployed senior engineers are abundant.
revenue_model: $1.5-4k per inspection at 40-50% gross margin, recurring contracts with portfolio buyers, and referral fees from repair shops.
non_obvious_insight: When production cost collapses, value shifts to attestation. Every asset that became cheap to produce (1970s housing, used cars, diamonds) spawned an independent inspector class. Nobody has yet set the trusted standard for AI-built software, and the inspectors' seniority is the moat, the same people the market calls redundant.
first_30_days: Offer discounted $500 inspections in acquisition-marketplace buyer forums and Indie Hackers. Recruit 6 laid-off senior engineers and run 10 inspections on live listings. Publish anonymised findings ('7 of 10 exposed user data') and sign one escrow or broker referral partner.

title: Genetic-Resource Provenance Ledger for Bio-AI
one_liner: Track which genetic resources and sequences, physical and digital, feed a company's models and pipelines, so it can prove Nagoya compliance today and estimate Cali Fund exposure tomorrow.
customer: Nature-sourced discovery and AI-model builders, starting with the ABS, sustainability and legal units of large pharma, enzyme, ag, food and cosmetics groups, plus sample-collecting AI biotechs such as those mining plants and microbes.
problem: Trend chain: sequence-trained foundation models (Evo 2 trained on 9.3 trillion nucleotides across the tree of life) and proprietary sampling programs (Basecamp's Trillion Gene Atlas, Enveda's sourcing) make genetic-resource provenance a first-class asset. The Cali Fund (launched Feb 2025) asks large DSI users for roughly 1% of profits or 0.1% of revenue, but had only two contributions totaling $6,000 by August 2026. COP17 (Yerevan, Oct 19-30, 2026) is due to confirm rates and allocation. Nagoya duties for physical samples already exist, and public sequence metadata on origin is sparse. Nobody instruments any of it.
solution: Software plus advisory. Ingest sample logs and training or data manifests. Map accessions to origin metadata, flag ABS status, model Cali Fund exposure scenarios, and generate audit-ready disclosures and a 'DSI provenance statement' for model cards. Broker PIC/MAT permit packages for new sampling. Phase 1 revenue comes from existing Nagoya duties on physical collections.
why_now: COP17 is weeks away, and national DSI rules may move faster than the fund. The fund's weak uptake means the near-term product must be Nagoya and provenance assurance, with DSI as an option that COP17 could harden.
revenue_model: $25-120k annual license or advisory for enterprises, $5-15k per collection-permit package, and one-off audit sprints.
non_obvious_insight: The DSI debate is framed as a tax question, but the scarce asset is the sequence-to-origin map. If COP17 or national laws harden, whoever holds the provenance graph sells compliance to everyone. If they do not, the same graph sells 'clean provenance' assurance to acquirers and pharma partners.
first_30_days: Build a lead magnet: a 'DSI exposure snapshot' of a public training corpus or a company's sequence set. Offer 10 free snapshots to sustainability and legal leads. Recruit 2 sample-collecting AI biotechs with live ABS contracts as design partners. Partner with an ABS law firm.

title: Courthouse-Handwriting Graph to Clear Heirs' Property
one_liner: Use AI that can read old handwritten deeds and probate files to map who really owns family land that never went through probate, and sell clean title to the buyers who need it.
customer: Solar, wind, pipeline and broadband developers, land trusts and conservation buyers, timber and ag buyers, and title insurers, with legal-aid partners protecting heirs.
problem: When a landowner dies without probate, title fragments among dozens of heirs. Developers can't lease or buy without consent, and heirs can lose land through partition sales. The records are handwritten across probate, deed and marriage files, so clearing one parcel takes lawyers weeks or months.
solution: LLM handwriting recognition over courthouse records builds a family-of-record graph per parcel, ranks probable heirs, finds them, and manages consent, lease or purchase packages through e-signature. Partner attorneys file quiet-title or partition actions for hard cases. Developers get a 'title-readiness score' per parcel. The design bakes in fair terms and legal aid for heirs.
why_now: Multimodal models now read historical cursive at near-human accuracy, and county records are increasingly scanned. The Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act has been adopted in a couple dozen states, which pushes toward consensual deals. The land rush for solar and data-center sites needs clean title fast.
revenue_model: $2K-$10K per cleared parcel paid by the developer or a percentage of lease value, plus data licensing to title insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The transfer that never went through probate, family land passed informally for generations, is a hidden inventory of blocked assets. Now a buyer with money (energy and data infrastructure) will pay to clear it.
first_30_days: Pick one county in a solar-active area with high heirs' property prevalence. Get a developer's list of blocked parcels. Process 10 parcels and partner with a heirs' property legal clinic to review the process and heir outreach.

title: Vet-Side Passport Network for Pets and Horses
one_liner: Give official veterinarians a certificate copilot that turns microchip-anchored records into error-free health certificates and a verifiable travel dossier that carriers and shippers can check before departure.
customer: Official Veterinarian practices in the UK and EU (and accredited vets in the US), plus pet and horse transport companies. Ferry, tunnel and airline operators are later payers for pre-verified manifests.
problem: Since 22 April 2026 UK-based owners must use single-entry Animal Health Certificates, 11-14 pages issued by an Official Veterinarian, instead of EU-issued passports. Vet time per certificate is heavy, the timing windows for vaccination and treatment are easy to get wrong, and a chip-number or wording error means refusal at the border. Horse shippers juggle TRACES, FEI and national passport systems separately.
solution: Software for vet practices that pulls microchip and vaccination data from practice-management systems, imports lab results, applies a country-rule engine with timing windows, pre-fills the certificate and flags errors before the vet signs. It issues the owner a portable dossier with a verifiable signature and QR code. A pre-flight checker lets shippers validate multi-animal consignments before departure.
why_now: The April 2026 EU rule change, wider TRACES digital processing, and constant UK-EU rule churn mean a maintained rules engine has recurring value. Owners are newly forced into per-trip certificates.
revenue_model: $100-190 per OV per month plus $10-20 per certificate, shipper plans from about $300 a month, and later per-manifest fees from carriers.
non_obvious_insight: The animal identity problem is already solved: microchips and horse life numbers are global standards. What is missing is trust and issuance friction, and a licensed vet is the human trust anchor. You do not need new identity infrastructure. You sell the trust anchor a better pen, and animals avoid the privacy fights that slow human wallets.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 OV practices near Dover and Folkestone, where certificate volume is highest, and 3 horse shippers. Start with the UK-to-EU Animal Health Certificate only, filling PDFs semi-manually. Charge per certificate, measure vet minutes saved and rejection rate, and publish the numbers to win the next 50 practices.

title: Bot-Proof Local Comments: Verified Neighbors, Pseudonymous
one_liner: Secret and Yik Yak died of unaccountable anonymity and Digg's March 2026 relaunch died of bots; the missing primitive is 'one real human, from this place, no real name', and local newsrooms and city councils will pay for it.
customer: Independent and nonprofit local newsrooms (hundreds exist) that have switched off comments, and city, county and school-board clerks running public comment for hearings on rezonings, data centers and levies.
problem: Newsrooms disabled comment sections because of toxicity and bots, so local conversation moved to Facebook groups. Public bodies get astroturf and AI-generated comment floods (the 2017 FCC net-neutrality docket was later found mostly fake by New York's attorney general) and cannot tell residents from out-of-area campaigns or bots.
solution: An embeddable comment and public-comment widget. Each person verifies once via a state mobile ID in Apple or Google Wallet with address check, or a postcard PIN or voter-file match as fallback, then posts under a pseudonym. The platform attests only 'verified human, resident of ZIP or ward X'. Public bodies get a verified-resident tally (for example, '412 verified residents commented, 78% opposed, 61 from Ward 3'). One credential works across the paper, council and school board, and publishers never see identity.
why_now: Digg's open beta launched 14 January 2026 and shut on 14 March 2026 after bot and AI-agent floods. Agents can now write plausible public comments at scale. Mobile IDs in phone wallets make cheap, high-assurance verification possible. Local news funders are paying for audience-trust infrastructure.
revenue_model: $200-1,500/mo per newsroom; $500-3,000/mo per municipality or agency for a verified public-comment portal; per-verification fees ($0.50-1.50) sponsored by foundations or civic funders; later, verified local polling panels.
non_obvious_insight: Anonymity was never the fatal flaw; unverifiable anonymity was. In a bot-saturated internet, 'provably a real neighbor' becomes the scarce good, and local institutions already need it but cannot buy it. The credential also compounds: a resident verified once for the newspaper is reusable for council, school board and library levy comments.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 small newsrooms through nonprofit-news networks to run a verified-comment pilot on one hot local issue (rezoning or data center) using SMS or postcard plus voter-file match. Publish the verified-tally story, then pitch the same town's clerk a public-comment pilot. Charge $250/mo after the pilot.

title: Settlement Claim Autopilot for Ticket Buyers
one_liner: A privacy-first app that reconstructs a fan's ticket purchase history and files claims in ticketing settlements and refund orders, paid per validated claim by administrators and plaintiff firms.
customer: Settlement administrators and plaintiff firms, who pay per validated claim because they are judged on claim rates. Consumers use it free or pay a success fee.
problem: The FTC alleges $3.7B in resale fees from 2019-2024. Live Nation was found liable on monopolization in April 2026. In June 2026 the UK CMA ordered StubHub to refund 50,000+ customers, and World Cup ticket failures triggered class actions in New York and British Columbia. Claim rates in consumer settlements are typically low because buyers cannot reconstruct old purchases.
solution: Fans forward receipt emails or upload data exports (avoiding restricted Gmail scopes at launch). Local parsing rebuilds each purchase (event, price, fee, date) and matches it to open claim windows and prefilled forms. Sell it to administrators as a claims-acquisition channel, and keep watching for new live-events settlements.
why_now: A wave of ticketing liabilities is landing at once, and cheap models can parse messy receipts. Individual recoveries of about $30 are uneconomical for lawyers but work in batch.
revenue_model: $3-15 per validated claim from administrators and law firms, optional 10-15% consumer success fee, and later expansion to other settlement categories.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer is the administrator or counsel measured on claim rate, not the consumer. Email receipts are better proof than memory, and automation turns tiny per-person recoveries into a scalable business.
first_30_days: Launch a landing page around the CMA StubHub refund order. Pitch 5 administrators and pilot one active claim. Test the receipt-forward parser with 500 users and negotiate a per-claim bounty.

title: CJIS 6.0 Identity Kit for Small Agencies
one_liner: A managed multifactor and identity-verification stack that works in patrol cars, radio dead zones and shared workstations, ready for the Oct 1, 2027 CJIS deadline.
customer: Sheriff's offices and police departments with 10-150 sworn officers and no dedicated IT security staff, plus the managed service providers that serve them.
problem: CJIS 6.0 requires MFA and identity verification by Oct 1, 2027. Generic MFA breaks on shared terminals, offline vehicles and old mobile data computers. Small agencies buy compliance piecemeal from a few vendors and fail audits.
solution: Hardware keys plus a cached-token offline mode and a shared-workstation login flow, with an agency-level compliance dashboard and audit-ready evidence. Onboard officers in minutes through mobile driver's license or badge-based identity proofing.
why_now: The deadline is fixed and less than 13 months out. Agencies are starting budget cycles now, and state CJIS systems agencies will begin enforcing.
revenue_model: $8-15 per user per month or a per-agency package of $6-30K per year, plus hardware sold at cost plus margin.
non_obvious_insight: The real customer is the MSP serving 50 small agencies. One channel partner delivers dozens of deployments, and offline behavior is the differentiator that enterprise identity vendors will not build.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 MSPs that serve sheriffs. Prototype offline token caching on a rugged laptop. Run 3 no-cost pilots in agencies with upcoming CJIS audits.

title: Posthumous Likeness Trusts for Creators
one_liner: Estate planning for people whose face and voice already earn money: who may license their AI replica, who may not, and how it is enforced.
customer: Mid-tier creators (100K-5M followers), podcasters, voice actors, and the small managers and MCNs who represent them.
problem: Consumer-grade video and voice cloning means anyone's likeness can be recreated after death. Laws are a patchwork (Tennessee's ELVIS Act and California's 2024 digital-replica laws, a federal NO FAKES bill pending). Creators' estates hold real income (channels, catalogs, sponsorships) but have no instrument to permit, forbid or license replicas. Platforms handle it ad hoc.
solution: A 'Likeness Trust Kit': (1) a will or trust addendum with a digital-replica directive (allowed uses, revenue splits, ban list, who decides), (2) a registry and notice system aimed at platforms and AI vendors, (3) monitoring for unauthorized replicas and template takedowns, (4) a channel-continuity plan (access, memorialization, pinned messages), and (5) an optional licensing desk for approved 'legacy' uses.
why_now: The fall-2025 backlash over AI videos of deceased public figures made estates' concerns public. State post-mortem publicity laws changed in 2024, and platforms have begun shipping likeness-detection tools for creators (verify current status). No estate product has priced in that a voice and face are now licensable and misusable assets.
revenue_model: $1,500-$3,500 setup for documents and registry, $19-$79/month monitoring, and 10-20% of licensed uses. Managers buy in bulk.
non_obvious_insight: Estate lawyers treat likeness as a celebrity issue. The willing buyers are working creators who already understand platforms and already earn from their persona, and they are numerous and reachable through managers.
first_30_days: Partner with an entertainment attorney. Draft a template addendum. Sell to 10 creator managers at about $2K per client. Use off-the-shelf detection tools for monitoring and publish a public 'creator death checklist' for lead generation.
